## Abstract

The 2011 discovery of the first rare earth–dependent enzyme in methylotrophic Methylobacterium extorquens AM1 prompted intensive research toward understanding the unique chemistry at play in these systems. This enzyme, an alcohol dehydrogenase (ADH), features a La^{3+} ion closely associated with redox-active coenzyme pyrroloquinoline quinone (PQQ) and is structurally homologous to the Ca^{2+}-dependent ADH from the same organism. AM1 also produces a periplasmic PQQ-binding protein, PqqT, which we have now structurally characterized to 1.46-Å resolution by X-ray diffraction. This crystal structure reveals a Lys residue hydrogen-bonded to PQQ at the site analogously occupied by a Lewis acidic cation in ADH. Accordingly, we prepared K_{142}A- and K_{142}D-PqqT variants to assess the relevance of this site toward metal binding. Isothermal titration calorimetry experiments and titrations monitored by UV–Vis absorption and emission spectroscopies support that K_{142}D-PqqT binds tightly (K_{d} = 0.6 ± 0.2 μM) to La^{3+} in the presence of bound PQQ and produces spectral signatures consistent with those of ADH enzymes.

The binding pocket of PQQ is circled in gray, and K_{142}, which occupies the same position as La^{3+} or Ca^{2+} in PQQ-dependent dehydrogenases is positioned following β6.

K_{142} is additionally poised within H-bonding distance of the carbonyl of C5, the C7 carboxylate, and the N6 atoms of PQQ and thus plays a key role in tethering PQQ in this binding site. Analysis of the structure (28, 29) highlights that to form these three contacts with PQQ, the sidechain of K_{142} adopts a sterically strained, and presumably high-energy, rotameric conformation (30). ### Metal Binding Affinities of Variants Assessed by ITC.

Quantitative measurements of Ca^{2+} and La^{3+} dissociation from each PqqT variant both with (Table 1) and without (SI Appendix, Table S4) PQQ bound were obtained by ITC. All data were handled in an identical manner by fitting to an independent binding model and including an added linear background correction to account for nonspecific interactions, as described in the Methods section and further in SI Appendix. From these experiments, we determined that the K_{d} for La^{3+} binding in PQQ ⸦ K_{142}D-PqqT is 0.6 ± 0.2 μM, an order of magnitude smaller than the K_{d}s measured for WT- or K_{142}A-variants. In contrast to this decrease in dissociation constant, the K_{d} for PQQ ⸦ K_{142}D-PqqT binding Ca^{2+} is 150 ± 30 μM, twofold larger than the K_{d}s measured for WT- or K_{142}A-variants. Comparing these data, we observe a 250-fold higher affinity for La^{3+} over Ca^{2+} in PQQ ⸦ K_{142}D-PqqT. One stark difference observed during the Ca^{2+} ITC experiments is that while the WT- and K_{142}A-PqqT variants maintain negative enthalpy changes during the titrations, the K_{142}D-PqqT variant showed a positive enthalpy change (Fig. 3). Ca^{2+} binding remained thermodynamically favorable in all variants; however, binding in PQQ ⸦ K_{142}D-PqqT became entropically driven by nearly doubling the entropy term relative to that observed in the WT- and K_{142}A-PqqT variants. A similar increase in entropy was observed in La^{3+} binding experiments with K_{142}A- and K_{142}D-PqqT; both show nearly a 50 J·mol^{−1}·K^{−1} increased in entropy change relative to WT-PqqT. One potential explanation for these observations is that upon modification of K_{142}, the PQQ pocket and adjoining tunnel can accommodate more water molecules that are displaced upon metal binding.

The dissociation constants of WT-, K_{142}A-, and K_{142}D-PqqT for La^{3+} in the absence of PQQ decrease from 500 ± 350 μM, to 200 ± 100 μM, to 25 ± 9 μM, respectively (SI Appendix, Figs S7–S9), while binding to Ca^{2+} was not observed for any variant (cite38†SI Appendix, Figs. S4–S6†www.pnas.org ). Given the impact of K_{142} mutations on these affinities, we hypothesize that the D_{142} residue and possibly the nearby E_{111}, D_{141,} and N_{143} residues may participate in metal binding (SI Appendix, Figs. S18 and S22). In line with this hypothesis, WT-PqqT only binds 0.2 ± 0.2 equivalents of La^{3+} in the absence of PQQ, while K_{142}A-PqqT and K_{142}D-PqqT each bind 1.1 ± 0.2 eq. La^{3+} (SI Appendix, Table S5). The data collected with WT-PqqT likely report on nonspecific interactions, mixing, and dilution. As discussed above, when PQQ is bound, both K_{142}A-PqqT and K_{142}D-PqqT have stronger affinities for both Ca^{2+} and La^{3+} (Table 1). This increase in affinity for both metal ions in the presence of PQQ indicates that each component contributes to the stabilization of the other within the binding pocket. Similar observations have been made in ADH enzymes, where metal ion coordination sites from both the protein and the PQQ cofactor contribute to binding and that both need to be present for metal binding to ADH enzymes (23, 24).

The present study examines the contribution of the ninth position of the Ca^{2+}-coordinating EF-loop to the tuning of Ca^{2+} affinity and selectivity, using the model EF-loop of the Escherichia coli galactose binding protein.
Using the spherical metal ions of groups Ia, IIa, and IIIa and the lanthanides as probes, both the Ca^{2+} affinities and ionic selectivities of the engineered sites are quantitated. Neutral side chains of different size at the ninth EF-loop position [Gln (wild type), Asn, Thr, Ser, Ala, Gly] are observed to yield similar Ca^{2+} affinities and retain the native ability to exclude the physiological competing metal cations Na^{+}, K^{+}, and Mg^{2+}. Acidic gateway side chains (Glu, Asp) are found to reduce Ca^{2+} affinity and shift the ionic charge selectivity as much as 10^{3}-fold toward trivalent cations. Relative to the native Gln, all engineered side chains cause a partial loss of ionic size selectivity, stemming from enhanced affinities for nonphysiological large ions. Overall, the results have implications for the molecular mechanisms used by the EF-loop to control both (i) charge selectivity, which is proposed to stem from the electrostatic repulsion between the coordinating oxygens, and (ii) size selectivity, which is theorized to involve complex interactions between multiple coordinating side chains. Finally, it has recently been shown that the ninth EF-loop position serves as a “gateway” to modulate the kinetics of Tb^{3+} binding and release without shifting the equilibrium affinity of this ion [Drake, S. K., & Falke, J. J. (1996) Biochemistry 35, 1753−1760]. The present results confirm that isoelectric substitutions at the gateway position have little effect on Ca^{2+} affinity, thereby supporting the hypothesis that the gateway side chain provides kinetic tuning of Ca^{2+} signaling proteins independently of their Ca^{2+} activation thresholds.

L233: ## Abstract
L234: Lanthanides (Lns) have been shown recently to be essential cofactors in certain enzymes in methylotrophic bacteria. Here we identify in the model methylotroph, Methylobacterium extorquens, a highly selective Ln^{III}-binding protein, which we name lanmodulin (LanM). LanM possesses four metal-binding EF hand motifs, commonly associated with Ca^{II}-binding proteins.
L235: In contrast to other EF hand-containing proteins, however, LanM undergoes a large conformational change from a largely disordered state to a compact, ordered state in response to picomolar concentrations of all Ln^{III} (Ln = La-Lu, Y), whereas it only responds to Ca^{II} at near-millimolar concentrations.
L236: Mutagenesis of conserved proline residues present in LanM's EF hands, not encountered in Ca^{II}-binding EF hands, to alanine pushes Ca^{II} responsiveness into the micromolar concentration range while retaining picomolar Ln^{III} affinity, suggesting that these unique proline residues play a key role in ensuring metal selectivity in vivo.
L237: Identification and characterization of LanM provides insights into how biology selectively recognizes low-abundance Ln^{III} over higher-abundance Ca^{II}, pointing toward biotechnologies for detecting, sequestering, and separating these technologically important elements.

L88: The biological importance of lanthanides, and the early lanthanides (La^{3+}–Nd^{3+}) in particular, has only recently been recognized, and the structural principles underlying selective binding of lanthanide ions in biology are not yet well established. Lanmodulin (LanM) is a novel protein that displays unprecedented affinity and selectivity for lanthanides over most other metal ions, with an uncommon preference for the early lanthanides.
L89: Its utilization of EF-hand motifs to bind lanthanides, rather than the Ca^{2+} typically recognized by these motifs in other proteins, has led it to be used as a model system to understand selective lanthanide recognition. Two-dimensional infrared (2D IR) spectroscopy combined with molecular dynamics simulations were used to investigate LanM’s selectivity mechanisms by characterizing local binding site geometries upon coordination of early and late lanthanides as well as calcium.
L90: These studies focused on the protein’s uniquely conserved proline residues in the second position of each EF-hand binding loop. We found that these prolines constrain the EF-hands for strong coordination of early lanthanides. Substitution of this proline results in a more flexible binding site to accommodate a larger range of ions but also results in less compact coordination geometries and greater disorder within the binding site.
L91: Finally, we identify the conserved glycine in the sixth position of each EF-hand as a mediator of local binding site conformation and global secondary structure. Uncovering fundamental structure–function relationships in LanM informs the development of synthetic biology technologies targeting lanthanides in industrial applications.
L92: ## Introduction
L93: In the last decade, certain members of the lanthanide series have been revealed to play unexpected, yet critical biological roles in the growth of methylotrophic (and some non-methylotrophic) bacteria.^{cite20†1 –cite21†3 } Beginning with the characterization of the first lanthanide-dependent enzyme, a methanol dehydrogenase,^{cite22†4 –cite23†6 } recent work has identified the first selective lanthanide-binding protein, lanmodulin (LanM),^{cite24†7 ,cite25†8 } as well as a system for lanthanide acquisition.^{cite26†9 –cite27†12 } Understanding how nature has evolved to use lanthanide elements – in particular, the light or “early” lanthanides (La–Nd) that organisms tend to prefer – is not only essential to uncovering the roles of lanthanides in biochemistry, but it could also lead to new biomolecule-based approaches for lanthanide separations and recycling in industrial applications.^{cite28†13 }
L94: LanM is of particular interest due to its ability to selectively bind lanthanides in vivo,^{cite24†7 } along with its utility in isolating lanthanides from other metals in industrial waste streams.^{cite29†14 } LanM is a unique EF-hand-containing protein (cite30†Fig.
L95: 1A ) with picomolar affinity and high selectivity for the lanthanide series, even over more abundant and available ions with similar ionic radii such as Ca^{2+}.^{cite24†7 } EF-hands consist of an entering helix, a ~12-residue metal-binding loop, and an exiting helix.^{cite31†15 } These metal-binding motifs are typically associated with Ca^{2+} binding proteins, such as calmodulin (CaM), the ubiquitous Ca^{2+} sensor protein.^{cite32†16 } Most EF-hands demonstrate a marginal preference for lanthanides over Ca^{2+},^{cite33†17 –cite34†19 } due to their higher charge.
L96: This feature has frequently been exploited in the laboratory as a method for the investigation of calcium binding.^{cite35†20 –cite36†23 } In the case of LanM, there is a remarkable 100-million fold selectivity for lanthanide binding over Ca^{2+} and other divalent metal ions.^{cite24†7 } This makes LanM an ideal model for understanding the relationship between EF-hand geometry and ion selectivity, as well as a scaffold for developing synthetic biological approaches for isolating lanthanides from other metals.^{cite28†13 ,cite29†14 } In particular, the structural principles underlying the significant affinity difference are not understood.
L97: Characterizing these principles deepens our understanding of lanthanide selectivity in biology and lays a foundation for designing LanM analogs with tailored ion-specific affinities. There are a few relevant observations that serve as a starting point for rationalizing the measured affinities: LanM undergoes a significant conformational change from disordered to ordered upon binding of three Ln^{3+} ions, to its EF-hands 1, 2, and 3 (the fourth EF-hand has very low lanthanide affinity).
L98: In the presence of Ca^{2+}, the protein’s conformational change is only partial and does not occur until nearly millimolar Ca^{2+} concentrations.^{cite24†7 } The NMR solution structure of the Y^{3+}-bound LanM^{cite25†8 } suggests that LanM’s metal sites may bind with a higher coordination number (8 or 9, depending on the site) compared to typical EF-hand/Ca^{2+} interactions (7 coordinate).^{cite31†15 } However, this method was unable to provide atomic-level detail of these binding sites, limiting the specific conclusions that can be drawn about lanthanide selectivity.

L107: The LanM EF-hand sequence is unique in several regards. Perhaps most distinctive is that each of LanM’s four EF-hands contains a proline in the second position of the binding loop, which is the first time this has been observed out of the hundreds of characterized EF-hand proteins.^{cite24†7 } This notable deviation from the highly conserved standard EF-hand motif^{cite39†24 } is thought to be a significant contributor to the lanthanide selectivity of LanM.
L108: This hypothesized function was initially investigated by constructing a variant of LanM with these four prolines mutated to alanine (4P_{2}A, cite30†Fig. 1B and cite30†C ).
L109: Whereas 4P_{2}A-LanM shows the same conformational response with similar apparent K_{d} values as the WT protein for La^{3+} and Nd^{3+} ions, this substitution both tightens the apparent K_{d} for Ca^{2+} binding and allows Ca^{2+} to induce the same, full conformational response as to Ln^{3+} ions.^{cite25†8 } These studies supported the proposed role of these prolines in lanthanide selectivity, but leave unanswered how the proline impacts metal ion coordination within the EF-hand.
L110: Vibrational spectroscopy directly accesses protein structure and conformational dynamics, including binding geometries, and is an established technique for investigating ion-dependent changes in coordination structure.^{cite40†22 ,cite41†25 ,cite42†26 } Specifically, the EF-hand glutamic and aspartic acid carboxylate vibrations, together with those of the backbone and side-chain amide carbonyls, are inherently spectroscopically sensitive to the ion radius, charge, and coordination geometry.
L111: The carbonyl stretching frequencies shift in response to changes in the local electrostatic environment.^{cite43†27 –cite44†29 } Furthermore, EF-hands natively contain both monodentate and bidentate carboxylate coordination geometries, the populations of which will shift depending on the charge and size of the coordinating ion.
L112: For example, these methods have revealed that Ln^{3+}-binding perturbs CaM’s binding site from its native Ca^{2+}-binding geometry, with a decrease in bidentate coordination and an increase in structural disorder.^{cite40†22 } Simulations of CaM bound to Eu^{3+} and Cm^{3+} also point towards increase in disorder, albeit with the opposite trend in bidentate coordination.^{cite45†30 } This contrast embodies the challenges of simulation and emphasizes the necessity of one to one comparisons between simulation and experiment.
L113: The accurate simulation of highly charged ions like trivalent lanthanides is a non-trivial aspect of this approach. Here we use Ln^{3+} force field parameters developed by Migliorati and coworkers^{cite46†31 } to simulate LanM complexed to three ionic conditions—divalent calcium, an early lanthanide represented by La^{3+}, and a late lanthanide represented by Lu^{3+}.
L114: These parameters were recently used to elucidate the structural characteristics, particularly water’s role, underlying a lanthanide binding tag (LBT) variant’s binding selectivity for certain lanthanides.^{cite47†32 }
L115: In the present study, we focus on sequence and metal ion-dependent differences in LanM by mapping the coordination geometries as reflected in IR lineshapes. We examine the biologically relevant early Ln^{3+} ions that LanM binds with the highest affinity (e.g., La^{3+}, Pr^{3+}, and Nd^{3+}), and the late Ln^{3+} ions that LanM also recognizes selectively but with weaker affinity (e.g., Tb^{3+} and Lu^{3+}), and Ca^{2+}, the typical substrate of EF-hands.
L116: We compare metal binding to WT LanM and to the 4P_{2}A variant, which is more Ca^{2+} responsive than the WT protein. These vibrational spectroscopy measurements are interpreted through simulations, which produce an atomistic representation of the ion size and charge effects on coordination.
L117: This approach directly links coordination ensembles with the high lanthanide affinities of LanM relative to well-studied EF-hand proteins, revealing ion-dependent structural characteristics underlying LanM’s remarkable selectivity.
L118: ## Methods
L119: ### Preparation of LanM for spectroscopic measurements
L120: Lanmodulin (LanM), both WT and the 4P_{2}A variant, were expressed and purified according to an established protocol, with Chelex treatment and exchange into 20 mM MOPS, pH 7.0.^{cite24†7 } Purified LanM was frozen in liquid N_{2} and lyophilized. The dried protein was deuterated by reconstituting in pure D_{2}O and incubating at room temperature for two hours before being frozen and lyophilized again.
L121: The deuterated LanM/MOPS lyophilisate was then dissolved in D_{2}O and pH-adjusted with DCl (Sigma-Aldrich, 99 atom% D) and NaOD (Sigma-Aldrich, 99 atom% D) to a pH reading of 6.5 uncorrected for deuterium effects.
L122: Protein buffer solutions were then combined with solutions of anhydrous metal chlorides (CaCl_{2}, LaCl_{3}, PrCl_{3}, NdCl_{3}, TbCl_{3}, and LuCl_{3}) in 50 mM deuterated MOPS/D_{2}O to give a final solution of 1.5 mM LanM and 5 mM metal ion to ensure saturation of LanM’s high-affinity binding sites, even in the case of Ca^{2+} (K_{d,app} = 710 μM for WT Ca^{2+}-LanM).^{cite24†7 } This final solution was once again adjusted to an uncorrected pH reading of 6.5.
L123: ### Two-dimensional infrared (2D IR) spectroscopy
L124: 2D IR spectra were collected with a custom-built 2D IR spectrometer described previously.^{cite40†22 } Briefly, the protein vibrational modes are excited by a pair of pump pulses resonant with the carboxylate asymmetric stretch, which are then probed by a third probe pulse.
L125: The excitation frequency is obtained by numerical Fourier transformation of the time delay between the two pump pulses, while the detection frequency axis is generated by measuring the probe and signal in the frequency domain using a grating-based spectrometer. Plotting the amplitude of the 2D IR signal for each pump frequency gives a spectrum analogous to absorption spectra.
L126: This pump-slice-amplitude (PSA) analysis method is described elsewhere.^{cite48†33 } All 2D IR spectra were collected at a fixed pump–probe waiting time of 150 fs. Pump and probe polarizations were set to the perpendicular geometry. Spectra were averaged over 5 million shots, or ~1.5 hours of acquisition. Pump scatter was minimized through phase cycling using a pulse shaper.
L127: ### Computational methods
L128: Simulations were carried out using CHARMM36 force field^{cite49†34 } and the TIP3P water model^{cite50†35 } as implemented in the GROMACS 2019.4 package.^{cite51†36 } Simulations were carried out starting with the Y^{3+}-bound NMR structure (PDB: 6MI5) which was energy minimized and equilibrated in a box containing ~6000 water molecules. Sodium ions were added to maintain charge neutrality.
L129: The structure of the 4P_{2}A-LanM variant was generated using the Pymol mutagenesis function starting from the same initial NMR configuration.
L130: Three MD potentials for different metal ion-bound forms were simulated in complex with LanM—a calcium ion using the CHARMM36 parameters for Ca^{2+}, as well as representative early and a late lanthanide ion generated using parameters for La^{3+} (σ_{LnO} = 3.310, ε_{LnO} = 0.4308) and Lu^{3+} (σ_{LnO} = 2.997, ε_{LnO} = 0.4308) developed by Migliorati et al.^{cite46†31 } The simulation box was equilibrated for 10 ns to solvate the protein before a 50 ns NPT production at 300 K and 1 bar using the Nose–Hoover and Parrinello–Rahman thermostat and barostat respectively.^{cite52†37 ,cite53†38 } Equilibration and convergence were confirmed via comparison of protein-ion distance distributions in the first and second halves of the production trajectory.
L131: ## Results and discussion
L132: ### 2D IR spectroscopy
L133: 2D IR spectroscopy is a useful technique to investigate protein structure and dynamics and has been applied to the study of metal-binding proteins such as CaM.^{cite54†39 –cite55†43 } Briefly, a 2D IR spectrum is represented along excitation and detection frequency axes. Lineshapes contain rich structural information.^{cite56†44 } Here we analyze spectra by extracting the excitation-axis contribution to the spectra using a pump-slice method. Pump-slice spectra (cite57†Fig.
L134: 2 ) were extracted from experimental 2D IR spectra of wild-type (WT) LanM and the (4P_{2}A) variant complexed with 3 equivalents of a representative series of early and late lanthanide ions, as well as Ca^{2+} (cite58†Fig. S1 and cite58†S2 , cite58†ESI‡ ).
L135: These spectra are analogous to IR absorption spectra and can be interpreted similarly.^{cite48†33 } Given the few binding site carbonyls in each protein, and the concentration range used in protein studies, obtaining adequate signal-to-noise ratio and proper background subtraction remains a challenge for IR absorption measurements, making 2D IR a useful alternative.^{cite55†43 ,cite59†45 ,cite60†46 } In combination with computational methods, 2D IR tracks the metal ion-dependent changes in coordination geometries and conformational disorder.

The apo spectra for both WT and the 4P_{2}A variant are similar, showing a single band centered at around 1595 cm^{−1} that is assigned to an unbound carboxylate asymmetric stretch.
L144: This feature can be observed in all of the spectra presented in the figure but is most pronounced for the late Ln^{3+} ions and Ca^{2+} with the WT protein, and generally becomes enhanced in the 4P_{2}A variant.
L145: EF-hand 4, which remains predominantly unbound due to its lower metal ion-affinity, may contribute to this unbound feature.^{cite25†8 } Metal-bound WT and 4P_{2}A LanM produce a second feature present in the 1610 cm^{−1} region, which is assigned to monodentate carboxylates.^{cite40†22 ,cite63†47 } Another notable feature in the Ca^{2+} bound 4P_{2}A spectrum is a low amplitude peak centered around 1558 cm^{−1}, a feature that has been observed in the natively Ca^{2+}-responsive EF-hand protein, CaM.^{cite40†22 } This feature is indicative of a bidentate carboxylate configuration.^{cite64†48 ,cite65†49 } Its presence in the 4P_{2}A but not the WT spectrum suggests that the proline produces Ca^{2+} binding configurations that are different from CaM or other EF-hand proteins.
L146: Previous studies have shown the bidentate feature to shift to lower frequencies (~1535 cm^{−1}) upon binding lanthanides instead of Ca^{2+} due to their increased charge.^{cite40†22 } This low-frequency feature is not visible in the Ln^{3+}-LanM spectra, which indicates that the bidentate carboxylate frequency in LanM may appear even lower, outside of the measured spectral range, and is therefore obscured on the low-frequency side by the OD bend vibration of water.^{cite66†50 ,cite67†51 } This interpretation is further supported by MD simulations, described below.
L147: Fitting the lineshapes to a combination of Gaussian functions semi-quantitatively describes the spectral features (cite58†Fig. S3 , cite58†ESI‡ ). Peak areas report the populations (i.e., number of residues) of the different coordination geometries, whereas peak frequencies report binding strength (i.e., strength of the electrostatic potential at the C=O positions). cite68†Table 1 shows the trend in the extracted center peak frequencies of the monodentate carboxylate asymmetric stretch.
L148: In the WT protein, decreasing lanthanide ionic radius is accompanied by a red shift of the monodentate feature. A higher center peak frequency has been correlated to stronger electrostatic interaction between ion and monodentate coordinating residues.
L149: For bidentate configurations, on the other hand, stronger interactions are accompanied by a shift towards lower frequencies.^{cite40†22 ,cite63†47 } As applied to LanM, this correlation may suggest that the metal–ligand interactions are optimal for the early Ln^{3+} ions but become weaker across the series, as well as in response to Ca^{2+} binding, perhaps due to the backbone’s inability to adopt favorable configurations given the smaller radii of the later Ln^{3+} ions.
L150: Conversely, in the case of the 4P_{2}A variant, frequencies are relatively independent of metal ion and the monodentate frequencies are generally red-shifted compared to WT. Therefore, although the 4P_{2}A mutation does not strongly affect lanthanide affinity and the native metal-dependent global conformational response, at least among the early Ln^{3+} ions,^{cite24†7 } the coordination environment of these lanthanides is perturbed relative to the WT.
L151: The Ca^{2+}-bound LanM monodentate peak frequency does not change with the 4P_{2}A mutation, suggesting that the Ca^{2+} binding configurations are similar, at least with respect to monodentate coordination. Together, these results support the hypothesis that proline residues in LanM’s EF-hands play an important role in creating a coordination environment uniquely suited for the early Ln^{3+} ions,^{cite24†7 } which are biologically relevant.^{cite69†5 ,cite70†10 ,cite28†13 ,cite71†52 }

L189: cite77†Open in a new tab L190: ### MD simulations
L191: Simulations produce an atomistic interpretation of the structural ensembles observed in the experiments, allowing for a more detailed residue-level analysis.
L192: This is a frequently utilized approach for investigating both protein structure and metal binding.^{cite78†53 –cite79†59 } Developing accurate models for lanthanide ions remains an active area of research.^{cite80†60 –cite81†65 } Lanthanide ion interactions with the hard ligands typical of protein lanthanide binding sites are largely driven by electrostatics.^{cite82†64 ,cite83†66 } We simulated three ionic conditions: Ca^{2+}, La^{3+}, and Lu^{3+}, to cover the range of ionic radii of the lanthanide series (cite76†Fig.
L193: 3B ).^{cite84†67 } The Y^{3+}-bound NMR structure^{cite25†8 } serves as the starting structure for our simulations. This method provides a tractable single-parameter model to directly capture the interplay between ionic radii and binding site structures. On the basis of prior biochemical and structural studies, the fourth EF-hand (cite30†Fig. 1A ) does not coordinate lanthanides with high affinity;^{cite24†7 ,cite25†8 } therefore, we focus on the carboxylate ligands of the first three binding sites.
L194: Within this structural analysis, each ligand is classified as monodentate, bidentate, intermediate, or unbound, using a two-step classification protocol. First, the α-carbon to ion distance of each ligand was calculated, with a distance larger than 0.4 nm being classified as “unbound,” selected by inspection of the histograms (cite58†Fig. S4 , cite58†ESI‡ ).
L195: Then, for each bound ligand, the difference in oxygen-to-ion distance was used to classify each ligand as monodentate (>0.1 nm), bidentate (0–0.05 nm), or unassigned (0.05–0.1 nm). These cut-offs were selected by examining the histograms shown in cite76†Fig. 3A and are consistent with values previously reported in the literature.^{cite85†68 } The resulting populations are shown in cite74†Table 3 . The populations of unassigned carboxylates is very small <2%.

L248: ## Abstract
L249: Lanthanide-binding tag (LBT) optimized for protein labeling was engineered into calmodulin by inserting a variant sequence (W_{7}Y_{8} → Y_{7}I_{8}) at Site 1 of the N-terminal domain while inactivating Site 2, and the resulting CaMLBT was examined for its Ln-binding properties. CaMLBT forms 1:1 complexes with all lanthanides.
L250: Fluorescence spectroscopy and CE-ICP-MS revealed dissociation constants ranging from sub-nanomolar for La (Kd = 437 ± 259 pM) to the low picomolar range for Tb–Lu, reaching Kd = 1.1 ± 0.4 pM for Lu at pH 6. This corresponds to a ∼1000-fold affinity increase over the original LBT, approaching the stabilities of lanmodulins. In contrast to lanmodulins, however, Ln–CaMLBT complex stability increases with decreasing Ln(III) ionic radius, consistent with trends reported for LBT.
L251: ATR-FTIR spectroscopy indicates that the enhanced stability arises from changes in coordination number and ligand properties: Glu_{9} would evolve from tight bidentate (La to Pr) to more asymmetric or weaker (Yb and Lu) coordination, while Asp_{3} and Asp_{5} evolve from pseudo-bridging to strong monodentate ligands. Notably, no evidence for water ligation was found for early lanthanides.
L252: CaMLBT emerges as a highly stable and versatile scaffold to investigate structural factors underlying lanthanide selectivity and complex stability.
L253: ## Graphical Abstract
L254: 
L255: Lanthanide affinity and selectivity in proteins remain poorly understood. Engineering calmodulin with a lanthanide-binding tag at Site 1 boosts affinity from nanomolar (isolated LBTs) to picomolar dissociation constants, comparable to lanmodulin but with distinct selectivity. ATR-FTIR indicates that site structuring within the protein and coordination reorganization govern this enhanced affinity and selectivity.
L256: ## 1 Introduction
L257: Lanthanides encompass lanthanum (La) and 14 elements, from cerium (Ce) to lutetium (Lu), in which the 4f orbital is progressively filled. These elements predominantly exist in the Ln(III) oxidation state in biological contexts, with notable exceptions such as cerium(IV) and europium(II).
L258: Unlike transition metals, where partially filled d-orbitals strongly interact with the ligand field, the 4f orbital in lanthanides is shielded by the outer 5s and 5p electrons, resulting in weak interaction with the ligand field. Consequently, ionic interactions primarily govern the reactivity of Ln(III) with coordinating ligands.
L259: Lanthanides are strong Lewis acids that favor binding to oxygen-donor ligands such as carboxylate, carbonyl, and hydroxyl groups and form strong interactions with water. Their relatively large ionic radii compared to transition metal cations of the same charge and the ionic character of their interactions result in a larger coordination number (7 to 12) and high coordination plasticity.
L260: Variations in Ln(III) coordination properties also results from the lanthanide contraction, the progressive decrease in effective ionic radius (IR) along the Ln series, from 1.16 Å for La(III) to 0.977 Å for Lu(III) for a coordination number of 8 [cite28†1 ]. This contraction can result in increased steric hindrance that in turn can reduce the coordination number.
L261: An increase in charge density and Lewis acidity also accompanies the IR contraction, progressing from the early lanthanides (La to Eu) to the late lanthanides (Gd to Lu), which results in shorter distances between the Ln and the first shell of coordinating atoms [cite29†2 , cite30†3 ].
L262: Ln(III) ions share similar properties and coordination preferences with calcium, suggesting that they can substitute Ca(II) in protein binding sites. Interactions of Ln(III) with Ca(II)-binding proteins have been extensively studied, and luminescent lanthanides such as Eu(III) and Tb(III) have been used to investigate the properties of Ca(II)-binding sites, notably in calcium-sequestering or calcium-sensing proteins of the EF-hand family, like calmodulin or troponin C [cite31†5 -cite32†13 ].
L263: Additionally, studies have focused on the E. coli galactose-binding receptor, which features a related Ca(II)-binding site [cite33†14 -cite34†16 ].
L264: Calmodulin contains the most prevalent Ca(II)-binding sites found in eukaryotes: the EF-hand helix-loop-helix motif. In this motif, calcium ligands are comprised within a twelve-amino-acid sequence, beginning with a nine-amino-acid long loop connecting two orthogonal α-helices and completed by three residues of the second α-helix (Scheme cite35†1A ) [cite36†4 ].
L265: The metal-binding sequences vary among EF-hand proteins and Ca(II)-binding sites, but Ca(II) is usually coordinated by seven oxygens in a pentagonal bipyramidal geometry, with ligands provided by residue side chains at positions 1, 3, 5, 9, and 12, where a Glu residue provides a bidentate ligand, and by the peptide carbonyl of the residue at position 7. Either residue 9 binds Ca(II) directly or it stabilizes a water molecule ligand of Ca(II), as in calmodulin Site 1 (Scheme cite35†1A ).
L266: Calmodulin has four EF-hand motifs organized into two pairs of sites located in N-terminal and C-terminal domains that exhibit different affinities for calcium and lanthanides, as well as intradomain and interdomain binding cooperativity [cite37†17 , cite38†18 ].

L272: The Ca(II) binding site of the EF-hand motif inspired the development of genetically encodable lanthanide-binding tags (LBTs) as powerful tools for in vivo imaging [cite40†19 , cite41†20 ]. Lanthanide ions, such as Tb(III), possess unique luminescence properties, low sensitivity to photobleaching, and long lifetimes (µs to ms), making them well-suited for in vivo imaging applications.
L273: LBTs were developed through directed combinatorial chemical synthesis and screening based on Tb luminescence, using the metal-binding sequence of Ca(II)-binding troponin C as a starting point. One of these LBTs, comprising 17 amino acids with the sequence YI-D_{1}TN_{3}ND_{5}GW_{7}YE_{9}GDE_{12}-LLA, exhibited apparent Ln-LBT dissociation constants in the micromolar to nanomolar range [cite41†20 ].
L274: The stability of the Ln–LBT complex increased as the Ln(III) ionic radius decreased, with dissociation constants ranging from 3.5 ± 0.2 µM for La to 57 ± 3 nM for Tb. Then, a slight decrease in stability was observed for lanthanides with shorter ionic radii than Tb, with dissociation constants increasing up to 128 ± 8 nM for Lu [cite41†20 ].
L275: High-resolution structural data of the Tb–LBT complex revealed that Tb is eight-coordinated with all ligands provided by the peptide, including the oxygens of monodentate Asp_{1} and Asp_{5}, bidentate Glu_{9} and Glu_{12}, and the carbonyl groups of Asn_{3} side-chain and Trp_{7} peptide backbone [cite41†20 ].
L276: An NMR and molecular dynamics (MD) study of the Ln-LBT complexes proposed that a water molecule coordinates early lanthanides instead of Asn_{3} side chain, explaining the lower stability of these complexes, while the high stability observed for the Tb–LBT complex was attributed to the absence of water in its coordination sphere [cite42†21 ].

L282: Recently, Ln(III) ions were identified as central metals for pyrroloquinoline-dependent methanol and alcohol dehydrogenases present in a large range of methylotrophic and nonmethylotrophic bacteria [cite44†22 -cite45†24 ], highlighting the biological relevance of lanthanides in living organisms. Three additional lanthano-proteins were identified in methylotrophic bacteria: the LanPepsy protein [cite46†25 ], LanD [cite47†26 ], and lanmodulin [cite48†27 , cite49†28 ].
L283: The function of lanmodulin remains unknown, but this protein has been widely studied for its unprecedented affinity and selectivity for Ln compared to Ca. Lanmodulin binds three Ln(III) ions in a cooperative manner, with ‘mean’ dissociation constants in the picomolar range and a fourth one with micromolar affinity [cite48†27 , cite50†29 ]. In lanmodulins, the Ln binding sites are reminiscent of that of the calcium EF-hand motif, with all Ln ligands situated on a loop of 12 amino acids flanked by α-helices.
L284: However, the Ln-binding sequences, as well as the length of the α-helices and intersite distances significantly differ in lanmodulins and calmodulins, resulting in a different overall structure. Lanmodulin forms a compact helical bundle with three central helices and the four EF-loops positioned at the periphery [cite49†28 , cite51†30 ]
L285: The affinity of lanmodulins for Ln(III) largely exceed those reported for calmodulins, the galactose-binding protein, or the LBT, which are in the micromolar to nanomolar range, and the selectivity across the lanthanide series is also different, with a strong affinity for early Ln [cite33†14 , cite34†16 , cite41†20 , cite48†27 , cite50†29 , cite52†31 ].
L286: The lanmodulin of Methylobacterium extorquens, MexLanM, showed only weak selectivity, with mean Kd,_{app} ranging from 5.3 ± 0.6 pM for La(III) and Nd(III) to 25 ± 4 pM for Ho(III) [cite48†27 , cite52†31 ], while lanmodulin from Hansschlegelia quercus Hans-LanM showed a stronger selectivity with Kd,_{app} ranging from 68 pM to 91 pM for La(III) and Nd(III) and strongly decreasing for Dy, with the binding of only one Dy with a Kd,_{app} = 2.9 nM [cite49†28 ].
L287: The metal-binding sequences of the two lanmodulins differ slightly, notably at positions 1 and 9. Asp_{9} stabilizes two water molecules that complete the coordination sphere of Ln in the Mex-LanM-binding sites [cite50†29 , cite51†30 ], while water molecules are absent in the Ln(III) coordination spheres in Hans-LanM, where Glu_{9} is directly involved in Ln(III) coordination [cite49†28 ] (Sup. Table 1).
L288: The different structural factors that govern the high affinity of EF-hand-binding motives for Ln and their intra-Ln selectivity remain not totally understood. The Ln-binding properties and selectivity of Hans-LanM was shown to depend on extended hydrogen-bonding networks and on a Ln(III)-dependent formation of dimers [cite49†28 ]. Finally, lanmodulin properties could also largely depend on its remarkable binding cooperativity [cite52†31 , cite53†32 ].
L289: Given the relative coordination plasticity of lanthanides and the predominant ionic nature of their interactions, the factors governing the protein-binding affinity and binding selectivity are difficult to fully understand.
L290: Different questions concern the role of the amino acid sequence directly involved in Ln binding, the presence of water ligands, the overall protein or peptide structure, and the role of binding cooperativity in determining the affinity of protein sites for Ln(III) as well as the selectivity for Ln(III) versus alkaline earth cations and intra-Ln(III) selectivity.
L291: In this study, we aimed to measure the affinity of the LBT tag for lanthanides when grafted onto the N-terminal domain of calmodulin in place of calmodulin Site 1 and compare the results obtained with the resulting CaMLBT with previous data on LBT and calmodulin or lanmodulin. We also analyzed the Ln-CaMLBT complexes using FTIR difference spectroscopy, which allowed to detail the properties of the Ln(III)-binding carboxylate ligands.
L292: The CaMLBT forms 1:1 complexes with Ln(III) with affinities in the subnanomolar (La(III)) to low picomolar range for Nd(III) and later lanthanides, an affinity three orders of magnitude greater than those previously reported for Ln-LBT complexes, and a similar selectivity.
L293: Structural analysis of the Ln-CaMLBT complexes using FTIR spectroscopy did not reveal differences in structural reorganization, differences related to water molecule(s) or Asn_{3} in the Ln(III) coordination sphere but pointed progressive changes in properties of the carboxylate-Ln coordinating groups of Glu and Asp within the Ln series.
L294: ## 2 Results and Discussion
L295: In this work, we investigated the interactions between Ln(III) and the N-terminal domain of Arabidopsis thaliana calmodulin, engineered to incorporate the LBT metal-binding sequence at Site 1 while inactivating the metal-binding capacity of Site 2. The resulting peptide referred to as CaMLBT is fully described in the Experimental Section.
L296: The metal-binding ability of Site 2 was suppressed by introducing alanine residues at positions 1–3, as previously reported for other one-site variants of the calmodulin N-terminal domain [cite54†33 -cite55†35 ]. The metal-binding sequence of Site 1 is illustrated in Scheme cite35†1 . Unlike the tryptophan and tyrosine present at positions 7 and 8 in the LBT metal-binding sequence, CaMLBT features tyrosine and isoleucine at these positions.
L297: These residues were chosen for stabilizing the metal-binding site in the calmodulin N-terminal domain, by contributing to an inter site β-sheet structure (Scheme cite35†1 [cite36†4 , cite56†34 ]).
L298: ### 2.1 Stoichiometry of the Ln-CaMLBT Complexes
L299: The stoichiometry of the Ln-CaMLBT complexes was analyzed using electrospray ionization mass spectrometry (ESI-MS). Samples containing 1 µM CaMLBT and 2 µM of various lanthanides in 20 mM ammonium acetate at pH 6.15 were injected in native mode. As shown in Figure cite57†1 , the primary peak for CaMLBT without lanthanides (Apo CaMLBT) is observed at 8492 Da, with two smaller peaks corresponding to sodium and potassium adducts, respectively.
L300: Although lanthanides were added at a 1:2 CaMLBT:Ln ratio, only 1:1 complex were detected with all lanthanides tested, along with a varying proportion of Apo CaMLBT across the lanthanide series in the ESI-MS spectra (Figure cite57†1 ). The relative proportion of Apo CaMLBT decreased from 55 and 51% for samples with La and Ce, to 36–39% with Pr to Sm, 25 and 28% with Eu and Gd, 17–23% with Tb to Yb, and the lowest ratio was observed in the sample with Lu, with 15% of Apo CaMLBT (Sup. Figure 1 and Sup. Table 2).
L301: This observation is consistent with lanthanides binding solely at CaMLBT Site 1. Additionally, the progressive increase in the relative intensity of the Ln-CaMLBT peak compared to that of Apo CaMLBT along the lanthanide series suggests a progressive increase in complex stability as the lanthanide ionic radius decreases.

L307: ### 2.2 Stability of Ln-CaMLBT Complexes
L308: The stability of the Ln-CaMLBT complexes was analyzed using fluorescence spectroscopy and capillary electrophoresis coupled to inductively coupled mass spectrometry (CE-ICP-MS). In both cases, nitrilotriacetate (NTA) was added as a competitor for Ln binding. The stability constants of the Ln-NTA and Ln-NTA_{2}^{3−} complexes are known [cite59†36 ], allowing the determination of conditional stability constants for the Ln-CaMLBT complexes.
L309: The presence of NTA in the solution also allowed to control the Ln speciation.
L310: #### 2.2.1 Tyr_{7} Fluorescence
L311: The Ln-binding affinity of CaMLBT was assessed by following the fluorescence intensity of the single tyrosine residue Tyr_{7} of CaMLBT located in the metal-binding loop of Site 1. Fluorescence intensity of Tyr_{7} was previously shown to efficiently probe uranyl and calcium binding to calmodulin Site 1 in engineered N-terminal domain of calmodulin [cite38†18 , cite54†33 ].
L312: Uranyl induced a clear quenching of Tyr fluorescence, while for calcium, Tyr_{7} fluorescence increase could be associated to the structural changes linked to Ca-binding to calmodulin Site 1. A similar enhancement of tyrosine fluorescence was observed monitoring the fluorescence of Tyr residues of the whole calmodulin upon Ca^{2+} binding [cite60†37 ].
L313: For CaMLBT, Tyr_{7} fluorescence also increased upon Ca(II) binding, and the binding isotherm corresponded to a Ca-CaMLBT dissociation constant Kd = 33.2 ± 4.5 µM (Sup. Figure 2). In contrast, we observed a clear quenching of Tyr_{7} fluorescence upon addition of Ce, Eu, and Yb and to a lower extent upon addition of Sm, Nd, Pr, and Gd (Figure cite61†2A,B and Sup. Figure 4-9,14).
L314: The addition of La and the heavy lanthanides Tb, Dy, Er, Tm, and Lu induced smaller changes in Tyr_{7} fluorescence (Figure cite61†2C and Sup. Figure 3,10–13,15). With the hypothesis that all Ln bind at the same site in CaMLBT, this can be rationalized by the differences in electronic and redox properties of the lanthanides that determine their capacity to quench Tyr_{7} fluorescence by energy transfer or photoinduced electron transfer from the Tyr excited state.
L315: For some Ln, the changes in Tyr_{7} fluorescence properties result mainly from changes in its microenvironment upon lanthanide binding. It is noteworthy that the peptide carbonyl group of the residue at position 7 was shown to participate in the lanthanide coordination in LBT [cite41†20 ]. Results obtained from triplicates are presented in Table cite62†1 .

L392: For the formation of the Ca–CaMLBT complex, two main positive bands observed upon Ca binding, at 1561 and 1430 cm^{−1}, are confidently assigned to the ν_{as} and ν_{s}(COO^{−}) modes of glutamate residue(s) bound to Ca in a bidentate mode, by comparison with literature data on calmodulin and parvalbumin [cite88†12 , cite91†54 ] and given the small value of Δ(ν_{as}-ν_{s}) = 131 cm^{−1}. L393: The corresponding ν_{s} mode likely contributes around 1402–1405 cm^{−1}, overlapping with the negative band of the corresponding mode of the ionic carboxylate groups of Apo CaMLBT, which is consistently observed at 1402 cm^{−1} in all spectra of Ln-CaMLBT. L395: #### 2.3.2 FTIR Spectrum Recorded with La-CaMLBT
L396: The FTIR spectrum recorded with La-CaMLBT is different. As discussed above for Ca-CaMLBT, the positive bands at 1532 and 1436 cm^{−1} indicate the presence of bidentate glutamate ligand(s) to La(III), with the low Δ(ν_{as}-ν_{s}) = 96 cm^{−1} suggesting a strong interaction of each carboxylate oxygen with the positively charged La(III) ion. A downshift of the ν_{as}(COO^{−}) mode frequency of bidentate glutamate is indeed expected upon Ca(II) substitution by Ln(III) [cite88†12 ].
L397: The large band width at 1532 cm^{−1} suggests the contribution of two groups, likely corresponding to bidentate binding of Glu_{9} and Glu_{12}.
L398: A second broad positive band is observed at 1571 cm^{−1} with a shoulder at ∼1578 cm^{−1} (Figure cite76†5 ). The band frequencies point to the ν_{as}(COO^{−}) mode of the two aspartates Asp_{1} and Asp_{5} of the binding loop. The corresponding ν_{s}(COO^{−}) mode is difficult to assign and could contribute at 1430–1386 cm^{−1}, corresponding to a Δ(ν_{as}-ν_{s}) comprised between 140 and 192 cm^{−1}.
L399: This value is close to that of aspartate groups in solution (170–180 cm^{−1}), and the frequency of the ν_{as}(COO^{−}) mode at 1571–1578 cm^{−1} is slightly lower than that of Asp in solution. These observations rule out pure monodentate binding of the aspartate ligands in La-CaMLBT. In a FTIR study of Ca^{2+} binding to bovine α-lactalbumin, Mizuguchi et al.
L400: (1997) [cite90†55 ] showed that bands at 1578 cm^{−1} (in ^{2}H_{2}O, but only modest upshifts are observed for ν_{as}(COO^{−}) modes in ^{2}H_{2}O [cite92†56 ]) and 1425 cm^{−1} corresponded to Asp residues binding to Ca^{2+} in a pseudo-bridging mode, i.e., with one oxygen atom coordinated to Ca^{2+} and the second forming an interaction with a water molecule.
L401: For La-CaMLBT, the bands at 1571–1578 cm^{−1} indicate that the aspartate residues bind as two pseudo-bridging ligands, in which one carboxylate oxygen could interact with a water molecule in a second coordination sphere or with a hydrogen-bonding group of the protein. Finally, bands at 1503 and 1602 cm^{−1} could correspond to the ν_{19}(CC) and ν_{8a}(CC) ring modes of a tyrosine side chain [cite80†44 ] and sign an effect of La binding on the side-chain properties of Tyr_{7} in the metal-binding loop.
L402: #### 2.3.3 Changes in the FTIR Spectra along the Ln Series
L403: Interestingly, the band at 1532 cm^{−1} broadens and then gradually splits into two peaks along the Ln series. With Ce and Pr, a broad band is observed at 1532–1534 cm^{−1} with a more pronounced shoulder at higher frequency; then, two positive bands are observed for Nd at 1546 and 1533 cm^{−1}, and for the rest of the Ln series.
L404: While the band frequency at 1530–1533 cm^{−1} remains almost constant along the Ln series until Lu (Figure cite76†5 ), the band at 1546 cm^{−1} gradually shifts to higher values, from 1546 to 1563 cm^{−1} along the Ln series. The effect can be divided in three groups, from Nd to Eu (1543–1545 cm^{−1}), from Gd to Dy (1550–1554 cm^{−1}), and for Yb and Lu (1561–1564 cm^{−1}).
L405: This splitting is accompanied by a broadening of the ν_{s}(COO^{−}) mode observed at 1437 cm^{−1} for La, with a shoulder more pronounced at 1449–1450 cm^{−1} from Nd to Tb and then an additional band at 1459 cm^{−1} from Dy to Lu.
L406: The splitting of the ν_{as}(COO^{−}) mode at 1532 cm^{−1} and the progressive upshift of one of the two resulting bands indicate that one of the glutamate residues maintains a bidentate interaction with Ln throughout the series, while the other glutamate forms a bidentate interaction with early lanthanides, which is progressively destabilized as the ionic radius of the Ln decreases, leading to more asymmetric and then to a weaker coordination with late lanthanides.
L407: This effect is particularly pronounced for the two Ln with the smallest ionic radii, Yb and Lu, for which the ν_{as}(COO^{−}) mode frequency is close to that of ionic Glu in solution.
L408: A progressive upshift of the ν_{as}(COO^{−}) mode frequencies is also observed for the bands assigned to Asp side chains, from 1578–1570 cm^{−1} for La and Ce to 1588–1582 cm^{−1} for Pr and Nd, 1605–1593 to 1609–1597 cm^{−1} for Sm to Tb, 1611–1602 cm^{−1} for Yb, and 1617–1610 cm^{−1} for Lu (Figure cite76†5 , Supp. Table 3). These bands are assigned to Asp_{1} and Asp_{5} of the Ln-binding loop.
L409: These upshifts are consistent with a more pronounced monodentate character of the carboxylate ligands with the decrease in Ln ionic radius.
L410: From La to Nd, the frequencies indicate a pseudo-bridging interaction, i.e., hydrogen bonding interactions of the noncoordinating carboxylate oxygen, possibly with water molecules or residues of the protein. From Sm to Lu, the frequencies are consistent with monodentate carboxylates as observed for Ln(III)-EDTA complexes [cite88†12 ].
L411: The frequency of the ν_{as}(COO^{−}) mode of EDTA carboxylates increased from 1592 cm^{−1} for the La(III)-EDTA complex to 1608 cm^{−1} for the Lu(III)-EDTA complex, indicating a stronger interaction with Ln(III) of smaller ionic radius [cite88†12 ], consistent with the increased Lewis acidity of the late Ln. Similar upshifts are observed for the ν_{as}(COO^{−}) mode of the Asp_{1} and Asp_{5} side-chains when the Ln(III) ionic radius decreases in the Ln(III)-CaMLBT complexes.
L418: In the X-ray crystal structure of the Tb–CaMLBT complex reported by Nitz et al. (2004) [cite41†20 ], the coordination sphere of Tb includes bidentate Glu_{9} and Glu_{12} side chains, monodentate Asp_{1} and Asp_{5}, the carbonyl group of the Asn_{3} side chain, and the main chain carbonyl of Trp_{7}, with no water molecules in the coordination sphere of Tb. The FTIR data presented here are in line with a similar coordination for Tb with CaMLBT, and we can suggest a similar coordination for Eu to Dy.
L419: For Ln with shorter ionic radius, the FTIR data, which suggest a strengthening and shortening of the Ln-Asp interactions, accompanied by a destabilization of one of the Ln(III) bidentate Glu interactions are in line with MD simulations performed by Hatanaka et al. (2020) [cite42†21 ], where they compare structural models of La-LBT_{3} and Lu-LBT_{3}.
L420: The carboxylate group of Glu_{12} superimposes in the two structural models and clearly forms a bidentate ligand to La or Lu, while the distance between Glu_{9} and Lu is significantly larger than that between Glu_{9} and La.
L421: In the same study, Hatakana et al. (2020) [cite42†21 ] propose that a water molecule enters the coordination sphere of La(III) and destabilizes the interaction between Asn_{3} and La(III), while for Ln with shorter ionic radius, the water molecule is progressively excluded from the metal coordination. They propose that the exclusion of the water ligand could explain the larger affinity of LBT for Ln(III) of shorter ionic radius.
L422: Direct interaction of water with the Ln could not be detected here, and we cannot identify changes associated with Asn_{3} since they superimpose with the infrared signature of peptide groups. We do not observe however changes across the Ln series in this spectral range that could be associated to different coordination of Asn_{3} for the different Ln.
L423: While the investigation of water molecules in the coordination sphere is feasible for Tb(III) and Eu(III) using time-resolved laser-induced fluorescence spectroscopy (TRLFS), a definitive conclusion on the presence of water molecules in the coordination sphere of the early lanthanides (La, Ce, and Pr), which are not amenable to TRLFS, will require an experimental X-ray structure.
L424: The FTIR data indicate that the increased stability of the Ln(III) complexes along the lanthanide series is associated with a decrease in coordination number, from CN = 8 for La to Nd, to CN = 7, and possibly 6 for Yb and Lu. The higher stability of the complexes formed by CaMLBT with the late lanthanides may be attributed to the strength of the two Ln(III)–monodentate Asp interactions, the ability of the metal-binding loop to reorganize around the smaller Ln(III) ions, and their higher Lewis acidity.
L425: Nevertheless, the nearly identical affinities observed for lanthanides from Tb to Lu suggest the presence of certain constraints that hinder complete reorganization and optimization of the coordination sites. The pronounced decrease in stability observed for Ln(III) ions with ionic radii greater than 1.1 Å may stem from the difficulty of expanding the metal-binding cavity, likely due to the extensive hydrogen-bonding network characteristic of the EF-hand motif.
L426: The influence of EF-hand metal-binding sequences on Ln(III)-binding affinity and selectivity has been formerly studied using various approaches. These include short peptides [cite93†57 -cite94†59 ], longer peptides stabilized by cysteine disulfide bridges [cite95†60 ], calmodulin metal-binding loops grafted onto protein scaffolds [cite96†61 ], and site-directed mutants of proteins such as troponin C or galactose-binding protein [cite33†14 , cite34†16 ].
L427: While LeClainche & Vita [cite95†60 ] demonstrated tunable Tb affinity (mM to nM range) by modulating the metal-binding sequence, short peptides generally exhibit low Ln affinity, likely due to specific constraints that hinder direct comparison with this study.
L428: Protein-based analyses offer valuable insights. In the E. coli galactose-binding protein, the affinity for Ln(III) at the Ca(II)-binding site varied by approximately two orders of magnitude across the Ln series [cite33†14 , cite34†16 ], with stability increasing progressively with the Ln atomic number (Kd(La) = 71 ± 5 µM to Kd(Lu) = 0.55 ± 0.04 µM).
L429: Substituting the residue at position 9 of the loop significantly impacted Ln selectivity: serine almost suppressed the selectivity, by increasing the affinity for larger Ln, glutamate shifted the binding optimum to Nd-Sm, and presented similar affinities for later Ln (Eu to Lu) [cite34†16 ].
L430: Structural data from troponin C, psoriasin, and lanmodulins (Mex-LanM and Hans-LanM) suggest that the residue at position 9 controls the presence of Ln-coordinating water molecules. In troponin C and psoriasin, Asp_{9} stabilizes a water molecule ligand of Tb(III) or Ho(III), respectively, through hydrogen bonding interactions [cite97†62 , cite98†63 ]. Similarly, in Mex-LanM, Asp_{9} stabilizes two water molecules in the Nd(III) coordination sphere.
L431: In contrast, Hans-LanM features Glu_{9}, which directly coordinates La(III) in a bidentate manner, excluding water molecules from the coordination sphere. This coordination shifts to monodentate when La(III) is replaced by Dy(III) [cite49†28 ].
L432: These data support a key role of Glu_{9} in the CaMLBT in defining the Ln-binding properties and selectivity. Glu_{9} may contribute to exclude water ligands from the Ln coordination sphere. Although direct bidentate coordination of Glu_{9} to the early Ln may stabilize these complexes, the absence of direct water ligands might contribute to a lower flexibility of the binding cavity for the early Ln with large ionic radii and weaker CaMLBT affinity for La to Nd.
L433: Other structural factors, such as the hydrogen bonding network involving both the ligands and nonbinding amino acids, probably also tune the Ln selectivity of the CaMLBT binding site.
L434: ## 3 Conclusion
L435: In this study, we demonstrate that grafting the LBT Ln(III)-binding sequence onto calmodulin Site 1 within the engineered N-terminal domain confers high affinities for lanthanides, with dissociation constants (Kd) ranging from the subnanomolar to low picomolar range. The stability of the resulting Ln(III)–CaMLBT complexes increases as the ionic radius of the lanthanide decreases, with a particularly pronounced effect for ions with radii from La to Nd.
